events.title: Safari announced at Macworld
events.summary: Steve Jobs unveiled Safari at Macworld San Francisco on January 7, 2003 — Apple's own browser built on the KHTML engine, replacing Internet Explorer as the Mac default.
events.about: Safari brought fast rendering and tight macOS integration, then spread to iPhone and iPad as the engine behind mobile web apps. Apple open-sourced its fork as WebKit, which Google later used to build Chrome — making Safari's engine lineage central to modern browsing.

narrative.whyChosen: Safari ended Microsoft's Mac browser monopoly and launched the WebKit engine era.
narrative.whyImportant: WebKit became the foundation for mobile browsing and eventually Chrome.
narrative.problemSolved: Mac users depended on a slow, outdated IE port; Apple needed a fast native browser for [OS] X.

events.title: SQL Slammer worm doubles internet traffic
events.summary: The [SQL] Slammer worm spread on January 25, 2003 — exploiting an unpatched buffer overflow in Microsoft [SQL] Server and doubling global internet traffic within minutes.
events.about: Slammer was only 376 bytes — pure propagation with no payload beyond replication. It knocked out 911 dispatch systems, ATM networks, and South Korean broadband. DBAs learned that exposing [SQL] Server to the internet without patches was catastrophic; the worm also popularized egress filtering and segmented database networks.

narrative.whyChosen: [SQL] Slammer was the fastest-spreading worm in history at the time of its release.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved database servers on public IPs were critical infrastructure vulnerabilities.
narrative.problemSolved: Nothing initially — a single UDP packet could compromise unpatched [SQL] Server instances worldwide.
